clue.text: Novelist went up to historian

parts.note: past tense of rise, as the sun went up
Thomas Babington Macaulay, author of The History of England

explanation.surface: A writer climbs the ladder to reach a great chronicler of the past.
explanation.definitionFit: Dame Rose Macaulay was an English novelist, author of The Towers of Trebizond.

clue.text: Audience for Victorian novelist at Royal Society

parts.note: Charles Reade, author of The Cloister and the Hearth
RS is the standard abbreviation for the Royal Society, Britain's scientific academy

explanation.surface: A Victorian author gives a talk to the assembled scientists of the Royal Society.
explanation.definitionFit: The people who take in a book are its public, the body for whom it is written.

clue.text: Stevenson club with dwindling membership?

parts.note: Robert Louis Stevenson wrote a story about a club whose members agree to be killed one by one, so its numbers fall

explanation.surface: A society founded by Stevenson that keeps losing its members.
explanation.walkthrough: In Stevenson's tale the club's members draw cards to decide which of them dies next, so its roll naturally shrinks.
explanation.definitionFit: Stevenson's story collection is titled after this club of people who want to end their own lives.

clue.text: How Marquéz wrote and realistically

parts.note: Gabriel García Márquez is the great practitioner of the style called magical realism; the clue asks for the adverb that pairs with realistically

explanation.surface: A question about the manner of the Colombian novelist's writing.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is a fill-in: Márquez wrote ___ realistically, turning the label 'magical realism' into two adverbs.
explanation.definitionFit: Magical realism blends fantasy into ordinary life, so the author wrote by enchantment as well as realism.

clue.text: What Nell Dunn's Joy never was

definitions.text: What Nell Dunn's Joy never was

parts.words: What Nell Dunn's Joy never was
parts.note: Joy is the heroine of Nell Dunn's novel Poor Cow; though called a cow, she is never intimidated

explanation.surface: A remark about the spirited heroine of a 1960s novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Nell Dunn's Poor Cow follows Joy, a young London mother; the clue plays on her being a 'cow' who is never browbeaten.
explanation.definitionFit: Joy stays defiant throughout, so she is never frightened into submission.

clue.text: British geological feature immortalized by Wodehouse

parts.note: UK, the United Kingdom, stands for British
a ridge is a long raised stretch of land

explanation.surface: A landmark of the British countryside made famous by P. G. Wodehouse.
explanation.definitionFit: Stanley Featherstonehaugh Ukridge is the scheming hero of a series of Wodehouse stories.

clue.text: Flying heart doctors

parts.note: winged cupids who fly about painting and decorating, and who treat the heart by making people fall in love

explanation.surface: Airborne cardiac surgeons rushing to an emergency.
explanation.walkthrough: The cupids of Italian art work on hearts with their arrows, so they are winged physicians of love.
explanation.definitionFit: Amorini are the little winged cupids of Renaissance painting and sculpture.

clue.text: Pinnacle of existence, due to brainwork, say

definitions.meaning: being at the summit of society or success
a work by John Braine, his sequel to Room at the Top

explanation.walkthrough: 'brainwork' reads as mental effort, but it is a work by the novelist John Braine.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means living at the peak of success, and it is also the title of John Braine's 1962 novel.

clue.text: Describing how I introduce little review with mixed gin

indicators.note: the I comes first and leads in what follows, so it introduces the next piece

parts.note: mag is a short form of magazine, a periodical review

indicators.note: the letters of gin are mixed up to give a new order

explanation.surface: Someone explains how they bring a small magazine together with a cocktail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mixed' scrambles the gin; 'introduce' has the I lead in the magazine. The definition reads as a participle: imaging something is describing it.
explanation.definitionFit: Picturing or portraying something in words or images is a way of rendering it.

clue.text: Piracy the and war gave place politics and -—too the law-lord (Emerson, English Traits)

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Piracy the and war gave place politics and -—too the law-lord (Emerson, English Traits)': an OCR jumble of Emerson's sentence with words missing and misordered, no scan to restore it.
annotationWithheld.clue: Piracy the and war gave place politics and -—too the law-lord (Emerson, English Traits)

clue.text: Strange, rigid lessons from radical feminist

indicators.note: strange signals that the letters of the following words are rearranged oddly

explanation.surface: A firebrand of the women's movement delivers some odd, inflexible teaching.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strange' rearranges RIGID LESSONS into the author's full name.
explanation.definitionFit: The Nobel laureate who wrote The Golden Notebook became an icon of the women's movement.

clue.text: Referring to a gray thought in a green shade?

definitions.text: Referring to a gray thought in a green shade?

parts.words: Referring to a gray thought in a green shade?
parts.note: a twist on Marvell's line 'a green thought in a green shade', with Thomas Gray, author of the Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard, in place of green

explanation.surface: A line about melancholy musing in a leafy garden.
explanation.walkthrough: Marvell's The Garden has 'a green thought in a green shade'; a thought of Gray's would be mournful like his Elegy.
explanation.definitionFit: Gray's most famous poem is an Elegy, so a Gray-like thought is mournful and lamenting.

clue.text: Even less reliable than Jack Dawkins?

definitions.text: Even less reliable than Jack Dawkins?

parts.words: Even less reliable than Jack Dawkins?
parts.note: Jack Dawkins is the Artful Dodger of Oliver Twist; being more dodgy than him is being more of a dodger

explanation.surface: A comparison with Dickens's young pickpocket.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack Dawkins is the real name of the Artful Dodger in Dickens's Oliver Twist; the comparative of dodgy echoes his nickname.
explanation.definitionFit: Dodgy means shady or untrustworthy, and the comparative means more suspect still.

clue.text: Characterized as ghastly good by Betjeman

definitions.text: Characterized as ghastly good by Betjeman

parts.words: Characterized as ghastly good by Betjeman
parts.note: John Betjeman's 1933 book on English architecture is titled Ghastly Good ___

explanation.surface: A description of something the poet laureate found both awful and fine.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is a fill-in for the title of Betjeman's book Ghastly Good Taste.
explanation.definitionFit: Betjeman's title mocks refined aesthetic judgment that has turned dreary and correct.

clue.text: Money gets suit back for suicidal poet

parts.note: lucre is money, especially ill-gotten

indicators.note: back tells us the word suit is written in reverse order

explanation.surface: Cash buys a returned suit for a despairing versifier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' reverses the suit. Lucretius is the poet traditionally said to have killed himself, hence 'suicidal'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman author of De Rerum Natura was said by Jerome to have taken his own life.

clue.text: Rich clone cobbled together from Holinshed, perhaps

indicators.note: cobbled together means roughly assembled, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A wealthy duplicate is patched up out of Tudor history.
explanation.definitionFit: Raphael Holinshed compiled the historical record Shakespeare drew on, so his work is an example of a year-by-year history.

clue.text: Susan Howatch's take on Icarus?

parts.note: Susan Howatch wrote a novel called The ___; Icarus flew too near the sun

explanation.surface: A novelist's retelling of the myth of the boy who flew too close to the sun.
explanation.walkthrough: Howatch's 1999 novel bears this title, which also describes Icarus soaring on his wax wings.
explanation.definitionFit: An ambitious person who aims at the top, as Icarus aimed at the sun, is a soaring success-seeker.

clue.text: "Find — out a sunny seat, / With babe and lambkin at her feet.. coleridge"

definitions.text: "Find — out a sunny seat, / With babe and lambkin at her feet.. coleridge"

parts.words: "Find — out a sunny seat, / With babe and lambkin at her feet.. coleridge"
parts.note: a fill-in from Coleridge's poem, where the missing word is an old dialect form for a grandmother

explanation.surface: Lines of Coleridge picturing an old woman sitting in the sun with a baby and a lamb.
explanation.walkthrough: Grannam is an archaic word for grandmother, used by Coleridge in this pastoral verse.
explanation.definitionFit: The old dialect term means the grandmother of the family, seated with the child.

clue.text: Paper size for a London apprentice

definitions.meaning: a traditional size of writing paper
Tudor London apprentices and citizens were nicknamed after the round woollen headgear they wore

explanation.definitionFit: It is an old name for a large sheet of paper, and a nickname for a London prentice from his low woollen headgear.

clue.text: Hymnodist in serene alexandrines?

indicators.note: in tells us the answer sits inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: A hymn writer composing in calm twelve-syllable lines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' points to the run inside sereNE ALExandrines.
explanation.definitionFit: John Mason Neale wrote and translated hymns such as Good King Wenceslas.

clue.text: Composer offers work of fiction to behold

parts.note: a novel is a long work of fiction
lo is an old word meaning look or behold

explanation.surface: A musician presents a novel for us to admire.
explanation.definitionFit: Ivor Novello wrote Keep the Home Fires Burning and many musicals.

clue.text: Bounder in song by Sidney

indicators.note: in places the bounder inside the song

parts.note: an aria is a song in an opera
a cad is a dishonourable man, a bounder

explanation.surface: A rogue appears in a song by a man named Sidney.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts the bounder inside the song. 'by Sidney' defines the romance as a work written by Sir Philip Sidney.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Philip Sidney's prose romance is set in this pastoral region of Greece.

clue.text: "When av'rice, luxury and ease / A - - generation please" (Allan Ramsay)

definitions.text: "When av'rice, luxury and ease / A - - generation please" (Allan Ramsay)

parts.words: "When av'rice, luxury and ease / A - - generation please" (Allan Ramsay)
parts.note: a fill-in from the Scottish poet Allan Ramsay, who mocks a pale generation weakened by drinking a fashionable hot infusion

explanation.surface: Ramsay's couplet attacking a soft and greedy age.
explanation.walkthrough: Ramsay describes the young as sallow-complexioned from too much of the drink from China.
explanation.definitionFit: The compound means having a pallid complexion, blamed on too much of the fashionable drink.

clue.text: Scott's "wise wight" was black

parts.note: Walter Scott's novel The Black ___ has a misshapen recluse whom the locals call the wise wight

explanation.surface: A remark that Scott's wise creature was dark.
explanation.walkthrough: Scott's The Black Dwarf centres on Elshie, a deformed hermit the countryfolk call the 'wise wight'.
explanation.definitionFit: Scott's hermit is a person of very small stature, hence the title.

clue.text: Inexperienced writers without serious failings?

parts.note: no means without, as in no money
vices are grave moral failings

explanation.surface: Beginning authors are blameless characters.
explanation.definitionFit: Newcomers to any craft are beginners, and writers starting out are such beginners.

clue.text: Tate's cure-all

definitions.meaning: Nahum Tate, poet laureate, wrote a poem in praise of tea with this title

explanation.definitionFit: Nahum Tate's 1700 poem on tea bears this name, and the word means a universal remedy.

clue.text: Possibly con lady (but not Artemis) in ancient city

indicators.note: possibly signals that the following letters may be arranged another way

explanation.surface: A swindling woman, though not the goddess, in an old Greek town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' rearranges CON LADY. The aside 'but not Artemis' recalls that the goddess, no lady to this city, sent the boar that ravaged it.
explanation.definitionFit: Calydon was a city of Aetolia in Greek legend, famous for the boar hunt.

clue.text: Parts were named in this city guide

definitions.meaning: Henry Reed's war poem Naming of Parts appeared in his 1946 collection of this title
a plan of an Italian city's streets

explanation.definitionFit: Reed's collection holds his poem Naming of Parts, and literally it is a street plan of a northern Italian town.
